cse-2015-3-cs-14.approach: Split the 20-bit address into tag | line | offset: 16-byte blocks give 4 offset bits, $2^{12}$ lines give 12 line bits, leaving 4 tag bits. Each field is a whole number of hex digits, so read them straight off.

steps.title: Field widths
steps.body: Address $= 20$ bits. Offset $= \log_2 16 = 4$ bits; line $= \log_2 2^{12} = 12$ bits; tag $= 20 - 12 - 4 = 4$ bits.

steps.title: Read the hex digits
steps.body:
$(E201F)_{16}$: 5 hex digits = 20 bits, one digit per 4 bits.

| Tag (4) | Line (12) | Offset (4) |
|---|---|---|
| E | 201 | F |

optionAnalysis.reason: Tag = top hex digit E, line = next three digits 201.
F is the byte offset (last digit), not the tag.
E20 takes the wrong three digits; the line field is digits 2–4, i.e. 201.
2, 01F mixes line and offset digits; the tag is the leading digit E.

pitfalls: Taking the offset digit F as the tag.
cse-2015-3-cs-14.verification: The next byte E2020 has line 202, offset 0 — consistent with E201F being the last byte (offset F) of line 201.

cse-2015-3-cs-15.approach: Solve $(A - I)v = 0$ directly; two independent equations fix the eigenvector up to a scalar.

steps.title: Form A − I
steps.body: $$A - I = \begin{bmatrix}0&-1&2\\0&0&0\\1&2&0\end{bmatrix}$$

steps.title: Solve
steps.body:
Row 1: $-y + 2z = 0 \Rightarrow y = 2z$.

Row 3: $x + 2y = 0 \Rightarrow x = -2y = -4z$.

With $z = 1$: $v = (-4, 2, 1)$, so eigenvectors are $\alpha(-4,2,1)$, $\alpha \ne 0$.

pitfalls: Sign slip in $x = -2y$.

steps.title: Power ordering
steps.body: Grammars handled: SLR ⊂ LALR ⊂ canonical LR(1).

steps.title: Ease of implementation
steps.body: SLR is easiest (LR(0) automaton + FOLLOW); canonical LR is the most powerful. Pair: (SLR, canonical LR).

SLR easiest, canonical LR most powerful ✓.

steps.title: Apply the formula
steps.body: $\alpha = \dfrac{n}{m} = \dfrac{2000}{25} = 80$.

cse-2015-3-cs-18.approach: Build the minimal DFA for "contains 0011" (4 progress states + 1 trap accepting state = 5) and swap accepting/non-accepting states; complementing a complete DFA keeps the state count.

steps.title: DFA for L
steps.body:
State $q_i$ = length of the longest prefix of $0011$ matched so far; $q_4$ (seen 0011) is a trap with self-loop on 0,1.

| State | on 0 | on 1 |
|---|---|---|
| $q_0$ | $q_1$ | $q_0$ |
| $q_1$ (0) | $q_2$ | $q_0$ |
| $q_2$ (00) | $q_2$ | $q_3$ |
| $q_3$ (001) | $q_1$ | $q_4$ |
| $q_4$ | $q_4$ | $q_4$ |

steps.title: Minimality
steps.body: Shortest suffixes reaching acceptance differ: from $q_0$ need 4 symbols, $q_1$ 3, $q_2$ 2, $q_3$ 1, $q_4$ 0 — all 5 states are distinguishable, so 5 is minimal.

steps.title: Complement
steps.body: Make $q_0..q_3$ accepting and $q_4$ non-accepting. Same 5 states, still minimal (distinguishability is preserved).

scene.caption: Complement: q0–q3 accept, q4 is a dead state

optionAnalysis.reason: 4 states cannot track 0–4 matched symbols (5 distinguishable classes).
Minimal DFA for L has 5 states; the complement has the same 5 ✓.

pitfalls: Forgetting that the complement needs a complete DFA (the trap state counts).
Wrong transition from $q_3$ on 0 (goes to $q_1$, since "0010" ends in "0").
cse-2015-3-cs-18.verification: Distinguishing suffixes: $q_i$ needs exactly $4-i$ more symbols to accept ($q_4$: 0), so no two states merge.

cse-2015-3-cs-19.approach: Run bottom-up build-heap (heapify from the last internal node). Only 100, at depth 3, violates the heap property, and it must climb to the root — so at least 3 swaps, and build-heap achieves exactly 3.

steps.title: Find violations
steps.body: 1-indexed: parent of $i$ is $\lfloor i/2 \rfloor$. Every parent ≥ child except 100 at index 13 (parent index 6 holds 15). Nodes 2, 4, 5 and their subtrees are already fine.

steps.title: Swap 1: index 6
steps.body: Heapify(6): children 9, 100 → swap 15 ↔ 100.

steps.title: Swap 2: index 3
steps.body: Heapify(3): 50 with children 100, 2 → swap 50 ↔ 100; 50 at index 6 has children 9, 15 — fine.

steps.title: Swap 3: index 1
steps.body: Heapify(1): 89 with children 19, 100 → swap 89 ↔ 100; 89 at index 3 has children 50, 2 — fine. Done.

steps.title: Lower bound
steps.body: 100 must reach the root from depth 3 and each swap moves it up one level, so $\ge 3$ swaps. Minimum $= 3$.

optionAnalysis.reason: 4 is more than needed; build-heap uses 3.
2 swaps cannot lift 100 from depth 3 to the root.

pitfalls: Counting comparisons instead of interchanges.
cse-2015-3-cs-19.verification: Final array 100, 19, 89, 17, 12, 50, 2, 5, 7, 11, 6, 9, 15 — every parent ≥ its children.

cse-2015-3-cs-20.approach: An FD $X \to Y$ is trivial exactly when $Y \subseteq X$; check each option's right side.

steps.title: Definition

steps.body: $\{P,S\} \to \{S\}$: $\{S\} \subseteq \{P,S\}$ ✓ trivial. The others have RHS attributes ($T$, $Q$) outside the LHS.

cse-2015-3-cs-21.approach: FP = UFP × CAF, where UFP = Σ count × weight and CAF = 0.65 + 0.01 ΣFᵢ.

steps.title: Value adjustment
steps.body:
14 factors: 4 not applicable (0), 4 with value 3, remaining $14-8 = 6$ with value 4.

$\sum F_i = 4(0) + 4(3) + 6(4) = 0 + 12 + 24 = 36$.

$CAF = 0.65 + 0.01 \times 36 = 1.01$.

pitfalls: Counting the remaining factors as 10 instead of 6.
Using CAF $= 0.65 + \sum F_i$ without the 0.01.

cse-2015-3-cs-22.approach: Check each TCP property: full-duplex yes; SACK exists as an option (RFC 2018); TCP is a byte stream, not a message stream.

steps.title: Statement by statement
steps.body:
I — true: data flows both ways on one connection.

II — false: the SACK option (RFC 2018) exists.

III — false: TCP does not preserve message boundaries; it is a byte stream.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: I is true while II and III are false, so only statement I is correct.

optionAnalysis.reason: III is false — TCP is a byte stream.
II and III are both false.

cse-2015-3-cs-22.verification: SACK-permitted is TCP option kind 4 and SACK is kind 5.

cse-2015-3-cs-23.approach: Rewrite set difference as intersection with complement: $X \setminus Y = X \cap Y'$ and $Y' \setminus X' = Y' \cap X$ — identical. Refute the rest with counterexamples.

steps.title: Prove D
steps.body: $Y' \setminus X' = Y' \cap (X')' = Y' \cap X = X \cap Y' = X \setminus Y$. True for all $X, Y$.

steps.title: Refute others
steps.body:
A: $X = \emptyset$ gives $|X| = 0$, $|X'| = 6$.

B: two disjoint 5-element sets need $5 + 5 = 10 > 6$ elements.

C: fails e.g. for $|X| = 1$ (the conjunction must hold for every pair).

optionAnalysis.reason: False: two disjoint 5-subsets need 10 elements, but $|S| = 6$.
False: it claims every $X$ has size 2 and every $Y$ size 3.

pitfalls: Reading C as a conditional; it is a conjunction under ∀.

cse-2015-3-cs-24.approach: Case on the speaker's type. A truth-teller's statement is true; a liar's is false. In both cases the biconditional forces the coin to be head.

steps.title: Type 1 (truthful)
steps.body: Statement is true and "I am telling the truth" $= T$, so $H \leftrightarrow T$ true $\Rightarrow H$ true: head.

steps.title: Type 2 (liar)
steps.body: Statement is false and "I am telling the truth" $= F$, so $H \leftrightarrow F$ must be false $\Rightarrow H$ true: head.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Either way the result is head.

optionAnalysis.reason: Tail is impossible for either type.
A Type 2 person also implies head.

pitfalls: Negating each part of the liar's statement instead of the whole biconditional.
cse-2015-3-cs-24.verification: Only $H = T$ is consistent with "statement value = speaker honesty" for both types.

cse-2015-3-cs-25.approach: In any binary tree, $n_0 = n_2 + 1$ (leaves = nodes with two children + 1).

steps.title: Derivation
steps.body: Nodes $n = n_0 + n_1 + n_2$; edges $n - 1 = n_1 + 2n_2$. Subtracting: $n_0 = n_2 + 1$.

pitfalls: Thinking single-child nodes change the count — they cancel out.
cse-2015-3-cs-25.verification: A root with two leaves has $n_0 = 2$, $n_2 = 1$ ✓.

cse-2015-3-cs-29.approach: Look for a dirty read followed by an early commit: T2 reads A written by uncommitted T1 and commits before T1 ends — that is non-recoverable.

steps.title: Dirty read
steps.body: T1 writes A at time 2; T2 reads A at time 7 while T1 is still active.

steps.title: Commit order
steps.body: T2 commits at 8; T1 fails after 9 and must be rolled back, so T2 used a value that never officially existed — but T2 is committed and cannot be undone.

steps.title: Verdict
steps.body: Recoverability requires $T_j$ to commit only after every $T_i$ it read from commits. Violated ⇒ S is non-recoverable; atomicity cannot be ensured.

optionAnalysis.reason: A committed transaction (T2) cannot be aborted.
Non-recoverable: T2 read T1's dirty A and committed first ✓.
T2 is already committed and cannot be aborted.
Not recoverable because of the dirty read + early commit.

pitfalls: Thinking a committed transaction can still be aborted to fix the problem.
cse-2015-3-cs-29.verification: Reads-from pair (T1 → T2 on A) with commit(T2) before T1 ends ⇒ recoverability fails.

cse-2015-3-cs-30.approach: Evaluate Y in both loops (X[0][i] = i = X[i][0]) and use C's row-major layout: a row is contiguous, a column is strided by n.

steps.title: Check S1
steps.body: Segment 1: $Y[i] = X[0][i] = 0 + i = i$. Segment 2: $Y[i] = X[i][0] = i + 0 = i$. Same ⇒ S1 true.

steps.title: Check S2 and S3
steps.body:
Row-major: address of $X[i][j] = \text{base} + (i n + j)\,s$.

Segment 1 walks row 0: offsets $0,1,\dots,n-1$ ⇒ contiguous (S2 true).

Segment 2 walks column 0: offsets $0, n, 2n, \dots$ ⇒ gaps of $n-1 \ge 1$ elements (S3 false).

optionAnalysis.reason: S3 is false (column access strides by $n$).

pitfalls: Assuming column-major (Fortran) layout.
cse-2015-3-cs-30.verification: $n = 2$: X stored as 0,1,1,2; row 0 = positions 0,1 (contiguous), column 0 = positions 0,2.

cse-2015-3-cs-31.approach: The string $c$ has two parse trees ($S \Rightarrow F \Rightarrow c$ and $S \Rightarrow H \Rightarrow c$), so G is ambiguous — and no ambiguous grammar is LL(1) or LR(1).

steps.title: Ambiguity
steps.body: $S \Rightarrow F \Rightarrow c$ and $S \Rightarrow H \Rightarrow c$: two leftmost derivations of $c$.

steps.title: LL(1) table
steps.body: $FIRST(F) = \{p, c\}$, $FIRST(H) = \{d, c\}$ share $c$ ⇒ $M[S, c]$ has two entries ⇒ not LL(1).

steps.title: LR(1)
steps.body: After shifting $c$ with lookahead \$, items $[F \to c\cdot, \$]$ and $[H \to c\cdot, \$]$ coexist ⇒ reduce–reduce conflict ⇒ not LR(1). Neither S1 nor S2 holds.

optionAnalysis.reason: The LL(1) table has a conflict on $c$.
LR(1) has a reduce–reduce conflict on $c$.
Neither parser handles this ambiguous grammar.

pitfalls: Thinking LR(1)'s extra power fixes ambiguity — no deterministic parser can.
cse-2015-3-cs-31.verification: Every LL(1) and LR(1) grammar is unambiguous; G is not.

cse-2015-3-cs-32.approach: Nested matches (outer $a^m \dots b^m$, inner $b^n a^n$) fit a stack; crossed matches ($a^m b^n a^m b^n$) do not.

steps.title: L1 — CFL
steps.body: $S \to aSb \mid aAb$, $A \to bAa \mid ba$: nested matching, generated by a CFG.

steps.title: L3 — CFL
steps.body: $a^{2n+1} b^n$: $S \to aaSb \mid a$ generates it ($n \ge 0$). Context-free (even a single counter suffices).

steps.title: L2 — not CFL
steps.body: Crossed dependencies, like $\{ww\}$. Pump $a^p b^p a^p b^p$: $vxy$ has length $\le p$, so it touches at most two adjacent blocks; pumping changes a block without its matching partner ⇒ not CFL.

pitfalls: Treating $L_2$ like $L_1$ — the order of matched blocks matters.
cse-2015-3-cs-32.verification: $L_1$ and $L_3$ have explicit grammars; $L_2$ fails the pumping lemma.

cse-2015-3-cs-33.approach: A homogeneous system has a non-trivial solution iff its determinant is 0; this circulant determinant factors as $-(p+q+r)(p^2+q^2+r^2-pq-qr-rp)$.

steps.title: Determinant
steps.body: $$\begin{vmatrix}p&q&r\\q&r&p\\r&p&q\end{vmatrix} = p(rq - p^2) - q(q^2 - pr) + r(pq - r^2) = 3pqr - p^3 - q^3 - r^3$$

pitfalls: A sign error in the middle cofactor of the expansion.

cse-2015-3-cs-34.approach: Draw each Gantt chart and add turnaround times (completion − arrival). SRTF is optimal for average waiting/turnaround time, so it should win — verify numerically.

steps.title: SRTF
steps.body:
A 0–3 (B arrives at 1 needing 6 > 2 left). B 3–4; at 4 C (4) < B (5) ⇒ C 4–8 (at 6 D needs 2 = C's remaining 2, no preemption). D 8–10, B 10–15.

TAT: A 3, B $15-1 = 14$, C $8-4 = 4$, D $10-6 = 4$ ⇒ $25$, avg $6.25$.

steps.title: Compare
steps.body: $6.25 < 6.75 < 7.25 < 8.25$ ⇒ Shortest Remaining Time is lowest.

pitfalls: Breaking the C/D tie at t = 6 the other way does not change SRTF's total (still 25).
cse-2015-3-cs-34.verification: Every schedule ends at 15 (total burst 15, no idle time); only the completion order changes the TAT sum.

cse-2015-3-cs-35.approach: Expand both sides: $4x + 3 = 8y + 3 \Rightarrow x = 2y$; then apply digit constraints ($x \ge 5$, $0 \le y \le 7$).

steps.title: Constraints
steps.body: Digit 4 needs base $x \ge 5$ ⇒ $2y \ge 5$ ⇒ $y \ge 3$. Octal digit: $y \le 7$.

pitfalls: Allowing $y = 2$ ($x = 4$), where 4 is not a valid base-4 digit.
